tagline: An old turnpike landscape between Flint Hill and the Blue Ridge
intro: Ben Venue Road passes through a rural historic district between Flint Hill and US 211, with views west to the Blue Ridge Mountains. The district covers more than 2,600 acres and entered the National Register of Historic Places in 2016.

Agricultural development began here in the mid-18th century, as wealthy Virginia families established farms along one of the region's first turnpikes. The landscape has retained its rural character. At Ben Venue, the brick main house was built between 1844 and 1846; the property also includes three brick cabins that housed enslaved people, a kitchen and a smokehouse.

In Washington, the old US 211 alignment follows Warren Avenue, Middle Street and Main Street. Flint Hill stretches along Route 522; Ben Venue Road leads south from the village toward US 211. Laurel Mills lies farther south in the county, on the Thornton River along Route 618.

moments.title: Washington
moments.text: Washington keeps the street grid and street names shown on its 1797 town plan. The General Assembly established the town in 1796; it became the seat of the newly created Rappahannock County in 1833. Malcolm F. Crawford built the courthouse and adjacent clerk's office. The courthouse is a two-story brick building in the Jeffersonian style. In 1975, the town gained National Register recognition and a local review board charged with preserving its historic character. The old US 211 route still runs through the town on Warren Avenue, Middle Street and Main Street.

moments.title: Flint Hill
moments.text: Flint Hill grew from a crossroads community dating to 1740. Its compact, linear village contains farm buildings, houses, churches and schools, with styles ranging from Federal and Greek Revival to Gothic Revival and Craftsman. Most of the village entered the National Register in 2012, including two miles of Route 522 between Wilson Branch Creek and Ben Venue Road. Flint Hill Baptist Church began with a frame-and-weatherboard section in 1854. The church was enlarged and remodeled in the 1890s; its later additions include an entrance tower with a belfry. The building also has six stained-glass windows.

moments.title: Laurel Mills
moments.text: The Thornton River supplied the water power that shaped Laurel Mills. The village's houses and commercial buildings developed with its mill industry, chiefly from the 1840s to the early 1900s. The woolen mill closed in 1927; its ruins represent the village's early-20th-century industrial architecture. The historic district, including the mill remains, joined the National Register in 2004. Three workers' houses date to approximately 1840, with wood frames and stone foundations; the mill owner's house occupied the bluff above the village. Buildings line a single road that curves sharply at the bluff near the district's western edge.
moments.notice: Notice the road's sharp curve at the bluff and the surviving mill ruins.
